claim: Anchoring proteins sequester kinases with their substrates to locally disseminate intracellular signals and avert indiscriminate transmission of these responses throughout the cell.
source: Anchoring proteins sequester kinases with their substrates to locally disseminate intracellular signals and avert indiscriminate transmission of these responses throughout the cell.
evidence: This is a general statement about anchoring proteins supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: A-kinase anchoring proteins (AKAPs) spatially constrain phosphorylation by cAMP-dependent protein kinases (PKA).
source: A-kinase anchoring proteins (AKAPs) spatially constrain phosphorylation by cAMP-dependent protein kinases (PKA).
evidence: This is a well-established concept in the field supported by scientific knowledge.

claim: Type-II PKA-AKAP18γ complexes are hetero-pentameric assemblies.
source: Electron microscopy and three-dimensional reconstructions of type-II PKA-AKAP18γ complexes reveal hetero-pentameric assemblies that adopt a range of flexible tripartite configurations.
evidence: This claim is supported by electron microscopy data and three-dimensional reconstructions presented in the manuscript.

claim: Type-II PKA-AKAP18γ complexes adopt a range of flexible tripartite configurations.
source: Electron microscopy and three-dimensional reconstructions of type-II PKA-AKAP18γ complexes reveal hetero-pentameric assemblies that adopt a range of flexible tripartite configurations.
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy observations and 3D reconstructions shown in the manuscript.

claim: Intrinsically disordered regions within each PKA regulatory subunit impart molecular plasticity that affords an ∼16 nanometer radius of motion to the associated catalytic subunits.
source: Intrinsically disordered regions within each PKA regulatory subunit impart the molecular plasticity that affords an ∼16 nanometer radius of motion to the associated catalytic subunits.
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis and measurements of particle radii presented in the manuscript.

claim: Manipulating flexibility within the PKA holoenzyme augmented basal and cAMP responsive phosphorylation of AKAP-associated substrates.
source: Manipulating flexibility within the PKA holoenzyme augmented basal and cAMP responsive phosphorylation of AKAP-associated substrates.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from in vitro phosphorylation assays and cell-based FRET measurements.

claim: The catalytic subunit remains within type-II PKA-AKAP18γ complexes upon cAMP elevation.
source: Cell-based analyses suggest that the catalytic subunit remains within type-II PKA-AKAP18γ complexes upon cAMP elevation.
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 5J and 5K.

claim: The dynamic movement of kinase sub-structures, in concert with the static AKAP-regulatory subunit interface, generates a solid-state signaling microenvironment for substrate phosphorylation.
source: We propose that the dynamic movement of kinase sub-structures, in concert with the static AKAP-regulatory subunit interface, generates a solid-state signaling microenvironment for substrate phosphorylation.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the structural and functional data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Intrinsically disordered regions of proteins are widespread in nature.
source: Intrinsically disordered regions of proteins are widespread in nature, yet the mechanistic roles they play in biology are underappreciated.
evidence: This is a statement based on established scientific knowledge in the field of protein structure.

claim: Disordered segments can act to link functionally coupled structural domains or orchestrate enzymatic reactions through allosteric mechanisms.
source: Such disordered segments can act simply to link functionally coupled structural domains or they can orchestrate enzymatic reactions through a variety of allosteric mechanisms (Dyson and Wright, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by Dyson and Wright, 2005.

claim: The regulatory subunits of protein kinase A contain functionally defined and structurally conserved domains connected by intrinsically disordered regions of defined length with limited sequence identity.
source: The regulatory subunits of protein kinase A provide an example of this important phenomenon where functionally defined and structurally conserved domains are connected by intrinsically disordered regions of defined length with limited sequence identity (Scott et al., 1987).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Scott et al., 1987.

claim: Phosphorylation of proteins is a universal means of intracellular communication that is tightly controlled within the spatial context of the cell.
source: Phosphorylation of proteins is a universal means of intracellular communication that is tightly controlled within the spatial context of the cell.
evidence: This is a general statement based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: Production of the second messenger cyclic AMP (cAMP) stimulates PKA to phosphorylate a range of cellular targets.
source: A classic example is production of the second messenger cyclic AMP (cAMP), which stimulates a cAMP-dependent protein kinase (PKA) to phosphorylate a range of cellular targets (Taylor et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Taylor et al., 2012.

claim: The PKA holoenzyme is a tetramer composed of two regulatory subunits (R) and two autoinhibited catalytic subunits (PKAc).
source: The PKA holoenzyme is a tetramer composed of two regulatory subunits (R) and two autoinhibited catalytic subunits (PKAc).
evidence: This is established knowledge about PKA structure.

claim: Binding of cAMP to each R subunit is believed to liberate active kinase and phosphorylation ensues.
source: Binding of cAMP to each R subunit is believed to liberate active kinase and phosphorylation ensues.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: The local action of PKA is dictated by A-kinase anchoring proteins (AKAPs) that impose spatial constraint by tethering this kinase in proximity to substrates.
source: The local action of PKA is dictated by A-kinase anchoring proteins (AKAPs) that impose spatial constraint by tethering this kinase in proximity to substrates (Wong and Scott, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wong and Scott, 2004.

claim: AKAPs organize higher-order macromolecular signaling complexes through their association with G-protein coupled receptors, GTPases and additional protein kinases.
source: AKAPs also organize higher-order macromolecular signaling complexes through their association with G-protein coupled receptors, GTPases and additional protein kinases.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge about AKAP function.

claim: AKAP-associated phosphatases and phosphodiesterases act to locally terminate signals.
source: Likewise, AKAP-associated phosphatases and phosphodiesterases act to locally terminate these signals.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about AKAP signaling complexes.

claim: Most AKAPs are large, intrinsically disordered macromolecules that lack recognizable structural domains.
source: Currently, structural details on PKA anchoring are limited because most AKAPs are large, intrinsically disordered macromolecules that lack recognizable structural domains.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge about AKAP structure.

claim: The central domain of AKAP18γ bears homology to bacterial 2H phosphoesterase domains.
source: An exception is the crystal structure of the central domain of AKAP18γ that bears homology to bacterial 2H phosphoesterase domains (Gold et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gold et al., 2008.

claim: High-resolution crystallographic structures of PKAc when free and in complex with the C-terminal autoinhibitory and cAMP binding domains of RI and RII have provided details on the mechanisms of catalysis and autoinhibition.
source: Likewise, high-resolution crystallographic structures of the catalytic subunit (PKAc) when free and in complex with the C-terminal autoinhibitory and cAMP binding domains of the type I or type II regulatory subunits of PKA (RI and RII) have provided details on the mechanisms of catalysis and autoinhibition (Knighton et al., 1991, 1992; Gold et al., 2006, 2008; Wu et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple crystallographic studies.

claim: A complete structural picture of the PKA holoenzyme is lacking despite decades of effort.
source: Yet, despite decades of effort, a complete structural picture of the PKA holoenzyme is lacking.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The lack of a complete PKA holoenzyme structure is presumably due to the presence of long flexible intrinsically disordered linker regions within the R subunit.
source: This is presumably due to the presence of long flexible intrinsically disordered linker regions within the R subunit that tether this complex.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural knowledge and the challenges in crystallography.

claim: The N-terminal domains of RI and RII homodimerize through a four-helix bundle docking and dimerization interface (D/D).
source: NMR spectroscopy and X-ray crystallographic studies show that the N-terminal domains of RI and RII homodimerize through a four-helix bundle docking and dimerization interface (D/D) (Newlon et al., 2001; Gold et al., 2006; Kinderman et al., 2006; Sarma et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple structural studies.

claim: The D/D domain creates a high-affinity binding groove for a canonical amphipathic helix on each AKAP.
source: The D/D creates a high-affinity binding groove for a canonical amphipathic helix on each AKAP that forms the reciprocal binding surface (Gold et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gold et al., 2006.

claim: Macromolecular assemblies were formed when purified human AKAP18γ was incubated with the PKA holoenzyme.
source: Macromolecular assemblies were formed when purified human γ isoform of AKAP18 (AKAP18γ) was incubated with the PKA holoenzyme (PKAholo), formed by the RIIα and PKAc subunits (Figure 1A, 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and described in Materials and methods.

claim: The AKAP18γ-PKA complex migrated as a single species with an apparent molecular weight in excess of 240 kD on native electrophoresis.
source: Native electrophoresis established that a majority of this material migrated as a single species with an apparent molecular weight in excess of 240 kD (Figure 1C, right).
evidence: This is supported by native gel electrophoresis data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The molecular mass of the AKAP18γ-PKA complex is consistent with a hetero-pentameric complex composed of a single AKAP18γ molecule anchored to an RIIα subunit dimer and two PKAc subunits.
source: This molecular mass is consistent with a hetero-pentameric complex composed of a single AKAP18γ molecule anchored to an RIIα subunit dimer and two PKAc subunits.
evidence: This is an inference based on the molecular weight determination from native gel electrophoresis.

claim: Single particle analysis of AKAP18γ-PKA complexes revealed clusters of three densities, each approximately 60–100 Å in size resembling beads on a string.
source: Single particle analysis revealed clusters of three densities, each approximately 60–100 Å in size resembling beads on a string (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 1D and 1E.

claim: The tripartite structures of AKAP18γ-PKA complexes adopted a range of conformations.
source: Closer inspection of individual particles established that these tripartite structures adopted a range of conformations (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy observations shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Class averages of AKAP18γ-PKA complexes revealed a remarkable variety of configurations ranging from a tightly packed pseudo-symmetric triangular configuration to a fully extended linear configuration.
source: Class averages revealed a remarkable variety of configurations (Figure 1F; Video 1). These ranged from a tightly packed pseudo-symmetric triangular configuration (Figure 1F, left panel) to a fully extended linear configuration of the three densities (Figure 1F, right panel).
evidence: This is supported by class average data shown in Figure 1F and Video 1.

claim: The central density of AKAP18γ-PKA complexes was consistently smaller (∼60 Å) than the two peripheral densities (85 × 100 Å).
source: In either case, the central density was consistently smaller (∼60 Å) than the two peripheral densities (85 × 100 Å).
evidence: This is supported by measurements from electron microscopy data.

claim: Affinity-labeling of strep-tagged AKAP18γ with a 5 nm gold particle targeted the smaller central density.
source: Affinity-labeling of strep-tagged AKAP18γ with a 5 nm gold particle targeted the smaller central density, indicating that this element includes the anchoring protein (Figure 1D, inset).
evidence: This is supported by gold-labeling experiments shown in Figure 1D inset.

claim: Three-dimensional reconstructions for the triangular and linear configurations of the AKAP18γ–PKAholo complex were determined at 35 Å resolution.
source: Three-dimensional (3D) reconstructions for the triangular and linear configurations of the AKAP18γ–PKAholo complex were determined at 35 Å resolution from a tilted-series dataset (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is supported by 3D reconstruction data shown in Figure 2A and supplementary figures.

claim: In the triangular conformation, the two peripheral densities are oriented at a 100° angle with respect to the central density and exhibit an end-to-end length of ∼300 Å.
source: In the triangular conformation, the two peripheral densities are oriented at a 100° angle with respect to the central density and exhibit an end-to-end length of ∼300 Å (Figure 2A, top).
evidence: This is supported by measurements from 3D reconstructions shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The end-to-end length of the AKAP18γ-PKA complex increases to ∼385 Å in the extended linear configuration.
source: The end-to-end length increases to ∼385 Å in the extended linear configuration (Figure 2A, bottom).
evidence: This is supported by measurements from 3D reconstructions shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The linear and triangular conformations of AKAP18γ-PKA complexes are structurally distinct.
source: Hence, we conclude that the linear and triangular conformations are structurally distinct.
evidence: This conclusion is based on back-projection analysis comparing the dimensions of the two conformations.

claim: The population of AKAP18γ-PKA complex structures followed a Gaussian distribution with a mean particle length of 275 ± 65 Å.
source: This population of structures followed a Gaussian distribution (Figure 2D, green trace) with a mean particle length of 275 ± 65 Å (n = 223).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of particle measurements shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Conformational plasticity observed in AKAP18γ-PKA complexes is facilitated by an intrinsically disordered region between residues 44 and 90 of RIIα.
source: We propose that conformational plasticity observed in these analyses is facilitated by this intrinsically disordered region between residues 44 and 90 of RIIα, a linker that connects the AKAP docking site (D/D domain) to the cAMP-responsive transduction domains.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on structural analysis and sequence alignment data.

claim: The linker regions of RIIα orthologs are of similar length but exhibit low amino acid identity.
source: This notion is further substantiated by a primary sequence analysis of RIIα orthologs, showing that the linker regions are of similar length but exhibit low amino acid identity (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Single-particle EM and class averages of assemblies formed with RIIα Δ44–86 yielded uniform complexes exclusively in a compact triangular configuration.
source: Single-particle EM and class averages of the assemblies formed with RIIα Δ44–86 yielded uniform complexes exclusively in a compact triangular configuration (Figure 3D,F).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 3D and 3F.

claim: Complexes formed with RIIα ZeChimera resembled the array of conformations observed for the wild-type AKAP18γ–PKAholo assembly.
source: In contrast, complexes formed with RIIα ZeChimera resembled the array of conformations observed for the wild-type AKAP18γ–PKAholo assembly (Figure 3E,G).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 3E and 3G.

claim: Particle radii for the RIIα Δ44–86 complexes ranged in length from 55 to 125 Å with a mean value of 87 ± 13 Å.
source: Particle radii for the RIIα Δ44–86 complexes ranged in length from 55 to 125 Å, (mean value of 87 ± 13 Å, n = 142; Figure 3H)
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Assemblies formed with the RIIα ZeChimera were extended with lengths ranging from 100 to 265 Å with a mean value of 168 ± 33 Å.
source: whereas the assemblies formed with the RIIα ZeChimera were extended with lengths ranging from 100 to 265 Å (mean value of 168 ± 33 Å, n = 296; Figure 3H).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3H.

claim: A flexible linker in RIIα is responsible for the conformational plasticity of the AKAP18γ–PKAholo assemblies.
source: Thus we conclude that a flexible linker in RIIα is responsible for the conformational plasticity of the AKAP18γ–PKAholo assemblies.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the experimental data comparing wild-type, deletion, and extended linker variants.

claim: The type 4 phosphodiesterase isoforms PDE4D3 and PDE4D5 associate with the central domain of AKAP18γ.
source: For example, the type 4 phosphodiesterase isoforms PDE4D3 and PDE4D5 associate with the central domain of AKAP18γ and are phosphorylated on two sites by PKA (Sette and Conti, 1996; Carlisle Michel et al., 2004; Stefan et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: PDE4D3 and PDE4D5 are phosphorylated on two sites by PKA.
source: For example, the type 4 phosphodiesterase isoforms PDE4D3 and PDE4D5 associate with the central domain of AKAP18γ and are phosphorylated on two sites by PKA (Sette and Conti, 1996; Carlisle Michel et al., 2004; Stefan et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: PDE4Ds co-precipitate with AKAP18γ and the RII subunits of PKA.
source: PDE4Ds co-precipitate with AKAP18γ and the RII subunits of PKA (Figure 4A, lane 1) but not with GFP controls (Figure 4A, lane 2).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: cAMP phosphodiesterase activity was enriched 3.27 ± 0.48-fold in AKAP18γ–GFP immune complexes as compared to GFP controls.
source: Accordingly, cAMP phosphodiesterase activity was enriched 3.27 ± 0.48-fold (n = 5) in AKAP18γ–GFP immune complexes as compared to GFP controls or samples treated with the PDE4 selective inhibitor rolipram (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by phosphodiesterase activity assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Phosphate incorporation into PDE4D was increased 1.87 ± 0.14-fold upon its tethering to AKAP18γ.
source: Phosphate incorporation into PDE4D was increased 1.87 ± 0.14-fold (p<0.05) upon its tethering to AKAP18γ as assessed by autoradiography (Figure 4D, E).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro phosphorylation assay data shown in Figure 4D and 4E.

claim: The proximity to a substrate afforded by AKAP18γ augments the cAMP-independent action of PKA.
source: This suggests that the proximity to a substrate afforded by AKAP18γ augments the cAMP-independent action of PKA.
evidence: This is an inference based on the increased basal phosphorylation observed in the presence of AKAP18γ.

claim: Basal PDE4D phosphorylation was enhanced 1.97 ± 0.18-fold in complexes formed with RIIα Δ44–86 when compared to a wild-type complex.
source: Basal PDE4D phosphorylation was enhanced 1.97 ± 0.18-fold (n = 6, p<0.05) in complexes formed with RIIα Δ44–86 when compared to a wild-type complex (Figure 4G, bars 1 and 4).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro phosphorylation assay data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Extension of the linker region in the context of AKAP18γ–RIIα ZeChimera PKAholo assembly had no effect on PDE4D phosphorylation as compared to wild type.
source: In contrast, extension of the linker region in the context of AKAP18γ–RIIα ZeChimera PKAholo assembly had no effect as compared to wild type (Figure 4G, bars 1 and 7).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro phosphorylation assay data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Addition of cAMP further augmented phosphorylation of PDE4D in all AKAP18γ-PKA complex variants.
source: Control experiments confirmed that addition of cAMP further augmented phosphorylation of PDE4D in all cases (Figure 4F, lanes 2, 5 and 8)
evidence: This is supported by in vitro phosphorylation assay data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Pretreatment with PKI inhibitor peptide abolished anchored kinase activity.
source: and pretreatment with PKI inhibitor peptide abolished anchored kinase activity (Figure 4F, lanes 3, 6 and 9).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro phosphorylation assay data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The AKAP can be thought of as a catalyst that physically brings the reactants together.
source: These data show that the AKAP can be thought of as a catalyst that physically brings the reactants together, and the flexibility within the anchored PKA holoenzyme allows for the precise orientation of the enzyme and substrate.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental data showing enhanced phosphorylation in AKAP complexes.

claim: Approximately 30% of PKA action represents cAMP-independent phosphorylation events.
source: This mechanism may be particularly relevant for cAMP-independent phosphorylation events that are believed to represent approximately 30% of PKA action (Taylor et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Taylor et al., 2012.

claim: AKAR-18RBS associates with wild-type RIIα and modified RIIα constructs.
source: As a prelude to these studies AKAR-18RBS association with wild-type RIIα or either of the modified RIIα constructs was confirmed by co-immunoprecipitation of each complex from HEK293 cells (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: mCherry tagged versions of each RIIα form were expressed to equivalent levels.
source: In parallel, immunoblot and confocal fluorescent imaging analyses confirmed that mCherry tagged versions of each RIIα form were expressed to equivalent levels (Figure 5C)
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: mCherry tagged RIIα forms were uniformly distributed in HEK293 cells.
source: and uniformly distributed in HEK293 cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The raw YFP/CFP emission ratio of AKAR-18RBS was elevated in unstimulated cells expressing RIIα Δ44–86 as compared to RIIα wild type or the RIIα ZeChimera.
source: The raw YFP/CFP emission ratio of AKAR-18RBS was elevated in unstimulated cells expressing RIIα Δ44–86 as compared to RIIα wild type or the RIIα ZeChimera (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by FRET measurement data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Cells expressing the more compact RIIα Δ44–86 form responded more rapidly and robustly to isoproterenol with a maximal FRET response at 200 s.
source: Importantly, cells expressing the more compact RIIα Δ44–86 form responded more rapidly and robustly to isoproterenol with a maximal FRET response at 200 s (Figure 5F,H, green trace).
evidence: This is supported by FRET measurement data shown in Figure 5F and 5H.

claim: The normalized FRET responses of the more compact and less flexible AKAR-18RBS-PKA complexes formed with RIIα Δ44–86 were significantly higher than those formed with wild-type RIIα or RIIα ZeChimera.
source: In contrast, the normalized FRET responses of the more compact and less flexible AKAR-18RBS-PKA complexes formed with RIIα Δ44–86 were significantly higher (Figure 5I, green, p<0.001).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of FRET data shown in Figure 5I.

claim: Removal of the flexible linker region in RIIα augments cAMP-responsive PKA phosphorylation of AKAR-18RBS inside cells.
source: Taken together, these cell-based studies indicate that removal of the flexible linker region in RIIα augments cAMP-responsive PKA phosphorylation of AKAR-18RBS inside the cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the FRET measurement data comparing different RIIα variants.

claim: Both the RII and C subunits of PKA were present in AKAR-18RBS immune complexes, even after stimulation of cAMP production by isoproterenol.
source: Interestingly, both the RII and C subunits of PKA were present in AKAR-18RBS immune complexes, even after stimulation of cAMP production by isoproterenol (Figure 5J, lanes 1 and 2).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5J.

claim: The C subunit was retained within the AKAP18γ complex upon isoproterenol stimulation regardless of whether the PKA holoenzymes were formed with wild-type RIIα, RIIα Δ44–86, or RIIα ZeChimera.
source: Again the C subunit was retained within the AKAP complex upon isoproterenol stimulation (Figure 5K, lanes 1 and 2). This occurred regardless of whether the PKA holoenzymes were formed with wild-type RIIα, RIIα Δ44–86, or RIIα ZeChimera (Figure 5K, top panel).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5K.

claim: Release of the C subunit from anchored PKA holoenzymes may not be required for the phosphorylation of nearby substrates.
source: A broader implication is that release of the C subunit from anchored PKA holoenyzmes may not be required for the phosphorylation of nearby substrates.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that C subunit remains associated with AKAP complexes after cAMP stimulation.

claim: Association with AKAPs limits and thereby defines the range of kinase action within the cell.
source: Under this scenario, association with AKAPs limits and thereby defines the range of kinase action within the cell.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural and functional data presented.

claim: The less flexible RIIα Δ44–86 dimer may constrain the PKAc subunits in a manner that minimizes the distance to their target substrate.
source: For example, the less flexible RIIα Δ44–86 dimer may constrain the PKAc subunits in a manner that minimizes the distance to their target substrate.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the enhanced activity observed with the deletion mutant.

claim: The more compact AKAP-PKAΔ44-86-substrate assembly may augment kinase activity by inhibiting the actions of signal termination enzymes.
source: Moreover, the more compact AKAP-PKAΔ44-86-substrate assembly may augment kinase activity by inhibiting the actions of signal termination enzymes.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the enhanced activity observed with the deletion mutant.

claim: Deletion of the flexible linker between residues 44–86 of RIIα enhances basal phosphorylation of anchored substrates.
source: Deletion of the flexible linker between residues 44–86 of RIIα not only enhances basal phosphorylation of these anchored substrates, but also supplements the catalytic efficiency of the anchored PKA holoenzyme in this cellular context.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the experimental data from in vitro and cell-based assays.

claim: The evolution of flexible linkers in RII may be a means to ensure bi-directional regulation of phosphorylation events by signal termination enzymes.
source: Hence, we propose that the evolution of flexible linkers in RII may be a means to ensure bi-directional regulation of phosphorylation events by signal termination enzymes.
evidence: This is a proposed evolutionary explanation based on the functional data.

claim: Extending the number of residues in the RIIα ZeChimera linker had little effect on the overall structure of the AKAP-PKA complex.
source: It is noteworthy that extending the number of residues in the RIIα ZeChimera linker had little effect on the overall structure of the AKAP-PKA complex, or on the activity of PKA monitored by our in vitro and cell-based assays.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the structural and functional data comparing the ZeChimera to wild-type.

claim: The average end-to-end length of random coil scales by the square root of the number of amino acids in the chain.
source: Moreover, this observation is consistent with theoretical analyses of random coiled chain models that demonstrate the average end-to-end length of random coil scales by the square root of the number of amino acids in the chain (average length ∼ N0.5, where N is the number of residues) (Flory, 1975).
evidence: This is supported by citation to theoretical work by Flory, 1975.

claim: Evolutionary constraint of the RIIα linker domain to 45–47 residues may ensure appropriate separation between the anchoring and transduction domains of anchored mammalian PKA holoenzymes.
source: Hence, evolutionary constraint of the RIIα linker domain to 45–47 residues may ensure appropriate separation between the anchoring and transduction domains of anchored mammalian PKA holoenzymes.
evidence: This is a speculative evolutionary explanation based on the structural and functional data.

claim: The array of conformations adopted by the anchored RII subunit dimer defines a 'radius of action' for the tethered catalytic subunit.
source: Another key element of our model is that the array of conformations adopted by the anchored RII subunit dimer defines a 'radius of action' for the tethered catalytic subunit.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the structural data showing conformational flexibility.

claim: The 'built in' flexibility within the PKA complex sets a dynamic range for basal and cAMP-dependent phosphorylation of nearby substrates.
source: Not only does this structural plasticity explain why an intact PKA holoenzyme structure has eluded X-ray crystallographers for over 20 years but also suggests that the 'built in' flexibility within this protein complex sets a dynamic range for basal and cAMP-dependent phosphorylation of nearby substrates.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the structural and functional data.

claim: The conformational variability of the tethered complex could enhance kinase access to multiple phosphorylation sites on the same substrate.
source: The conformational variability of the tethered complex could enhance kinase access to multiple phosphorylation sites on the same substrate, or, alternatively, orient each catalytic subunit toward distinct substrate proteins within the vicinity of the scaffolding site.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the functional significance of conformational flexibility.

claim: Static protein–protein interactions act in concert with the dynamic movement of sub-structures to orchestrate local phosphorylation events.
source: Our structural and cellular characterization of higher-order AKAP assemblies emphasizes how static protein–protein interactions act in concert with the dynamic movement of sub-structures to orchestrate local phosphorylation events.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings and proposed model.

claim: cAMP binds to the R subunits avidly with a KD of 6–8 nM.
source: Yet, cAMP binds to the R subunits avidly (KD 6–8 nM), and its rate of release is so slow that it is not readily apparent how the cAMP-binding sites turnover within the cell (Poppe et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Poppe et al., 2008.

claim: There is a report that cAMP can activate PKA without C subunit release.
source: Additionally, there is a report that cAMP can activate PKA without C subunit release (Yang et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yang et al., 1995.

claim: Particles of linear and triangular conformations remained clearly distinguishable at high tilt angles.
source: However, inspection of particles at various tilt angles showed that particles of linear and triangular conformations remained clearly distinguishable, even at high tilt angles (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by tilted-series electron microscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: When the triangular model is tilted completely on its edge its dimensions (max length = 300 Å) are significantly smaller than the maximum end-to-end length obtained for the linear reconstruction (max length = 385 Å).
source: Moreover, this back-projection analysis demonstrated that when the triangular model is tilted completely on its edge (where it may appear more linear in projection) its dimensions (max length = 300 Å) are significantly smaller than the maximum end-to-end length obtained for the linear reconstruction (max length = 385 Å).
evidence: This is supported by back-projection analysis of the 3D reconstructions.

claim: The central density of AKAP18γ-PKA complexes corresponds to 60 × 60 × 80 Å.
source: In both 3D reconstructions, a central mass with dimensions of 60 × 60 × 80 Å (corresponding to the site of AKAP18γ as demonstrated by affinity gold labeling, Figure 2A, black triangle and Figure 1D, inset) was flanked on either side by larger densities of 100 × 100 × 85 Å (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by measurements from 3D reconstructions shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The flanking densities in AKAP18γ-PKA complexes are each 100 × 100 × 85 Å and can accommodate a sub-complex of RIIα and PKAc.
source: was flanked on either side by larger densities of 100 × 100 × 85 Å (Figure 2A). These flanking densities can each accommodate a sub-complex of RIIα and PKAc.
evidence: This is supported by 3D reconstruction data and molecular modeling shown in Figure 2A.

claim: A primary function of AKAPs may be to ensure basal phosphorylation of tethered substrates.
source: Accordingly, a primary function of AKAPs may be to ensure basal phosphorylation of such tethered substrates.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of enhanced basal phosphorylation in AKAP complexes.

claim: Physiologically relevant PKA targets such as aquaporins or phospholamban require continual or instantaneous phosphorylation to fulfill their biological roles.
source: This could explain why physiologically relevant PKA targets such as aquaporins or phospholamban, which require continual or instantaneous phosphorylation to fulfill their biological roles, have their own AKAP-associated pool of kinase (Henn et al., 2004; Lygren et al., 2007; Gold et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on aquaporins and phospholamban.
